title: Electrolysis Calculations
short: Charge equals current times time; divide by Faraday's constant to count moles of electrons.
trouble: Students forget how many electrons each ion needs, so they predict twice as much copper as can form.

blocks.html: Electrolysis is stoichiometry with electrons as a reactant. The current tells you how many electrons pass, and the half-reaction tells you how many each ion needs. From there, moles to grams as usual. This builds on electrolytic cells.

Charge $q = It$ (coulombs = amperes × seconds). Moles of electrons $= q/F$, with $F = 96\,485\ \text{C/mol}$. Moles of product = moles of electrons ÷ electrons per formula (from the half-reaction). Mass = moles × molar mass.

An ampere is one coulomb per second, so current times time is total charge. One mole of electrons carries $96\,485\ \text{C}$ (Faraday's constant, $N_A$ times the charge of one electron). Each $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ needs two electrons to become a copper atom, so a mole of electrons makes only half a mole of copper. Michael Faraday found this pattern by experiment in the 1830s: the same charge always deposits amounts of different metals in proportion to molar mass divided by ionic charge.

blocks.cap: Silver plating at 0.500 A for 1789 s (about 30 min) deposits about 1.00 g of silver.

blocks.title: Copper plating
blocks.q: A current of $2.00\ \text{A}$ runs for $30.0\ \text{min}$ through $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$ solution. What mass of copper plates out?

blocks.title: How long?
blocks.q: How long must $0.500\ \text{A}$ run to plate $1.00\ \text{g}$ of silver?
steps: Moles of Ag $= \dfrac{1.00}{107.87} = 9.27 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$. $\mathrm{Ag^+ + e^- \to Ag}$: one electron each, so $9.27 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol}$ of electrons.

blocks.title: Aluminum on an industrial scale
blocks.q: How much charge is needed to make $1.00\ \text{kg}$ of aluminum from $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$?
steps: Moles of Al $= \dfrac{1000}{26.98} = 37.1\ \text{mol}$; three electrons each: $111\ \text{mol}$ of electrons.
$q = (111)(96\,485) = 1.07 \times 10^{7}\ \text{C}$. That is why aluminum smelters sit near cheap electricity.

blocks.html: Battery capacity is often given in ampere-hours, a unit of charge: $1\ \text{A·h} = 3600\ \text{C}$. A phone battery rated $3.0\ \text{A·h}$ can deliver $10\,800\ \text{C}$, about $0.11\ \text{mol}$ of electrons, before it needs recharging.

In practice some current is lost to side reactions, such as making hydrogen at the cathode, so real yields are slightly below the Faraday's-law amount. Industry reports this as the current efficiency.

Forgetting how many electrons each ion needs, which predicts twice as much copper as can form. Check the half-reaction every time: $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ takes 1, $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ takes 2, $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ takes 3.
